choices: Keep it — the destructor already deletes the pointer, so nothing leaks
Wrap it in a `std::shared_ptr` so ownership stays safe if the service is ever copied
Use a `std::unique_ptr` (via `std::make_unique`) instead of manual new/delete
Store it as a `raw_ptr<>` so any dangling use is detected at runtime
explain: Avoid manual `new`/`delete`. Use `std::unique_ptr`, stack variables, or member initializer lists like `predictor_(std::make_unique<...>(extractor))`.

prompt: A class receives a `PrefService*` from its factory; the `PrefService` is owned by the profile. A teammate stores it as `std::unique_ptr<PrefService> prefs_` "to be safe". What's the right review comment?
choices: Don't wrap an unowned resource in an ownership type; it will double free
Fine, as long as `prefs_` is declared last so it's destroyed first
Use `std::shared_ptr` instead so the profile and the class can share it
Fine, but call `prefs_.release()` in the destructor to avoid a double delete
explain: If a class doesn't own a resource, don't create ownership wrappers for it — doing so is a common source of crashes.

prompt:
Two objects need to share ownership of a cache. A teammate writes:

```cpp
std::shared_ptr<Cache> cache_;
```

What's the best response?
choices: Approve; `std::shared_ptr` is the standard C++ tool for shared ownership of a cache
Approve only if `std::make_shared` constructs it, so the control block is co-allocated
Replace with `std::weak_ptr` on both sides so neither object keeps the cache alive
`std::shared_ptr` is banned; use unique ownership, or `scoped_refptr` if truly needed
explain: `std::shared_ptr` is on Chromium's banned features list. Prefer unique ownership; use `base::RefCounted` / `scoped_refptr` only when shared ownership is truly needed.

prompt: Which `Shutdown()` implementation follows the standard for a class with a `weak_factory_` and pending async callbacks?
choices: Nothing is needed; the `WeakPtrFactory` destructor handles it
explain: Call `weak_factory_.InvalidateWeakPtrs()` at the *start* of shutdown, otherwise pending callbacks can fire on a partially-destroyed object.

choices: Replace the WeakPtr with `base::Unretained`, since the request outlives the callback
Nothing; WeakPtr dereferences are automatically no-ops when invalidated
Add `DCHECK_CALLED_ON_VALID_SEQUENCE` and an early `if (!request_) return;`
Wrap the call in a try/catch so an invalid pointer can't crash the process
explain: Always check a `base::WeakPtr` is valid before dereferencing, especially after async operations, and add thread checkers to methods using WeakPtrs.

prompt: A new class needs to hand out weak pointers to itself. Which declaration follows the standard?
choices: `class MyClass : public base::SupportsWeakPtr<MyClass> {};`
`class MyClass { std::weak_ptr<MyClass> self_; };`
`class MyClass { base::WeakPtrFactory<MyClass> weak_factory_{this}; };` as the first member
`class MyClass { base::WeakPtrFactory<MyClass> weak_factory_{this}; };` as the last member
explain: Use a `base::WeakPtrFactory<T>` member (declared last) instead of inheriting `base::SupportsWeakPtr<T>`; the factory performs more safety checks.

choices: Bind a member method directly: `BindOnce(&MyService::OnGetNetworkName, weak_this, ...)`
Capture `this` in the lambda instead of a WeakPtr, since the service owns `rpc_`
Keep it — the lambda's `if (!self)` check already makes it safe and readable
Bind `base::Unretained(this)` into the lambda instead, saving the null check entirely
explain: With WeakPtrs in async callbacks, bind to a member function so the call is auto-cancelled if the WeakPtr is invalid; don't capture the WeakPtr in a lambda.

prompt:
A teammate needs to run a blocking file read and then update UI state:

```cpp
base::ThreadPool::PostTask(
    FROM_HERE,
    base::BindOnce(&MyClass::ReadAndUpdate, base::Unretained(this)));
```

What should the reviewer suggest?
choices: Switch to `base::BindRepeating` so the task can be retried if the read fails
Keep `Unretained` but add a `SEQUENCE_CHECKER` to `ReadAndUpdate` to catch misuse
Capture a raw `this` in a lambda instead, since `Unretained` is just a wrapper for it
Post a static blocking function with `PostTaskAndReplyWithResult`; reply via a WeakPtr
explain: Never use `base::Unretained` when posting to thread pools — it leads to use-after-free. Run the blocking work on the pool and handle the result on the main thread via `PostTaskAndReplyWithResult` with a WeakPtr.

prompt:
A class owns a `base::RepeatingTimer timer_` and starts it like this:

```cpp
timer_.Start(FROM_HERE, delay,
    base::BindRepeating(&MyClass::OnTimer,
                        weak_factory_.GetWeakPtr()));
```

A reviewer is deciding what to comment. What's appropriate?
choices: Flag it as a bug: owned timers must use `base::Unretained(this)`, never a WeakPtr
At most a nit that `Unretained(this)` is preferred for an owned timer; not a bug
Flag it as a bug: owned timers can fire after destruction, so add `InvalidateWeakPtrs()`
Require `base::ThreadPool::PostDelayedTask` instead, so the timer isn't needed
explain: For a self-owned timer, `base::Unretained(this)` is preferred because the timer dies with the class. Using a WeakPtr is just overhead — a style preference, never a correctness bug, and never insist on changing it.

prompt:
A class owns `mojo::Remote<mojom::Foo> remote_` and sets:

```cpp
remote_.set_disconnect_handler(
    base::BindOnce(&MyClass::OnDisconnect,
                   base::Unretained(this)));
```

An automated review bot flags `base::Unretained` here as a potential UaF. Your call?
choices: Agree; Mojo disconnect handlers must always bind a WeakPtr, even when owned
Agree; bind `base::DoNothing()` and poll `is_connected()` instead
Disagree; `this` owns the endpoint, so it can't fire after destruction
Agree; move the remote into a `std::unique_ptr` so its lifetime is explicit
explain: `base::Unretained(this)` in disconnect/error handlers is safe when the class owns the `mojo::Remote`/`Receiver`/`AssociatedRemote` — the endpoint is destroyed with the class.

prompt: Which member ordering follows the standard?
choices: Ordering doesn't matter as long as members are alphabetized
explain: Place owning members (like `std::unique_ptr<>`) first and unowned `raw_ptr<>` members after them; it follows Chromium convention and makes ownership visually clear.

prompt: You need to act on a set of tabs after an async fetch completes. You currently have `std::vector<raw_ptr<Tab>> tabs`. What should you bind into the callback?
choices: `std::move(tabs)` — `raw_ptr` detects dangling pointers, so binding it is safe
A `std::vector<base::WeakPtr<Tab>>` built from each tab's `GetWeakPtr()`
A `std::vector<Tab*>`, avoiding `raw_ptr` overhead inside the callback
A `base::span<raw_ptr<Tab>>` over the vector, so nothing is copied
explain: Never capture `std::vector<raw_ptr<T>>` in async callbacks — the pointers may dangle by the time it runs. Bind a `std::vector<base::WeakPtr<T>>` instead.

prompt: A single-threaded class has a `SEQUENCE_CHECKER(sequence_checker_)`, but only 2 of its 10 methods call `DCHECK_CALLED_ON_VALID_SEQUENCE`. Best review comment?
choices: Apply the check to all methods or drop the checker; partial checking misleads
Fine; only the methods that touch shared state need the sequence check
Replace the checker with a `base::Lock` so every method is protected, not just two
Move the two checked methods into a separate class with its own checker
explain: Use `SEQUENCE_CHECKER` consistently — all methods or none. Partial checking is misleading and makes correct code look unsafe.

prompt: A `KeyedService` owns a fetcher and a database handle, and releases them only in its destructor. What's the guidance?
choices: That's correct; the destructor is the idiomatic RAII place for this cleanup
Move cleanup to a static `atexit` handler so it runs after all services
Release them in `Shutdown()` too, for orderly service-graph teardown
Release them lazily on first use after shutdown has been signalled
explain: For `KeyedService`s, clean up owned resources in `Shutdown()`, not just the destructor — the service graph has dependencies that require orderly teardown.

prompt: A `KeyedService` observes prefs via a `PrefChangeRegistrar` member and another source via `base::ScopedObservation`. Its `Shutdown()` is empty. A teammate says "ScopedObservation unsubscribes automatically, so we're fine." Response?
choices: Agreed; ScopedObservation and the registrar both clean up in the destructor, which is enough
Agreed, but add a DCHECK in the destructor that no observers remain registered
Replace ScopedObservation with manual `AddObserver` calls in the constructor only
Call `pref_change_registrar_.RemoveAll()` and `observation_.Reset()` in `Shutdown()`
explain: `ScopedObservation` can still lead to UaF: other services can trigger callbacks during their shutdown after yours. Always explicitly unsubscribe observers and pref registrars in `KeyedService::Shutdown()`.

prompt: You're adding a service under `components/` that needs prefs and network access. Which constructor follows the standard?
choices: `MyFeatureService(content::BrowserContext* context, scoped_refptr<network::SharedURLLoaderFactory> factory);`
`MyFeatureService(PrefService* prefs, scoped_refptr<network::SharedURLLoaderFactory> factory);`
`MyFeatureService(Profile* profile, scoped_refptr<network::SharedURLLoaderFactory> factory);`
`MyFeatureService(content::WebContents* web_contents, PrefService* prefs);`
explain: Component services should take specific dependencies like `PrefService*` and a URL loader factory, not `BrowserContext` — that prevents iOS reuse and adds content-layer dependencies.

prompt: A method `OnDataLoaded()` is only ever invoked via `base::BindOnce(&MyClass::OnDataLoaded, weak_factory_.GetWeakPtr())`. What should it contain to follow the standard?
choices: A `DCHECK_CALLED_ON_VALID_SEQUENCE(sequence_checker_)` at the top
A `base::AutoLock` around the whole body, since callbacks may run concurrently
Nothing extra; `BindOnce` with a WeakPtr already guarantees the right sequence
A `CHECK(this)` at the top to catch an invalidated WeakPtr
explain: Methods used as `base::BindOnce` / `base::BindRepeating` targets should include `DCHECK_CALLED_ON_VALID_SEQUENCE` to ensure they run on the correct thread.

choices: Make it `inline` instead of `static` so there's one copy across TUs
It's fine because it's `const`, so it's initialized at compile time
Return a function-local `static const base::NoDestructor<std::map<...>>`
Allocate it with `new` and never delete it, avoiding exit-time destructors
explain: Chromium prohibits globals with non-trivial destructors. Use `base::NoDestructor` as a function-local static (or `constexpr` for simple arrays/values).

prompt: `ContentScraper::Process()` does blocking work and is used from the UI thread. Callers currently each post manually to the thread pool and bind weak pointers. What does the standard suggest?
choices: Make `Process()` run synchronously on the UI thread with `ScopedAllowBlocking`
Make `ContentScraper` ref-counted (`RefCountedThreadSafe`) so it can be shared across threads
Use `base::Unretained` for all the posted tasks, since the scraper outlives them
Hold a `base::SequenceBound<ContentScraper>` and use `AsyncCall(&ContentScraper::Process)`
explain: For blocking/IO classes accessed asynchronously from the UI thread, use `base::SequenceBound<T>`: it binds the object to a task runner and posts all calls there automatically.

prompt: Which thread-pool post follows the standard for non-urgent work that can safely be abandoned at shutdown?
choices: `base::ThreadPool::PostTask(FROM_HERE, {base::MayBlock(), base::TaskPriority::BEST_EFFORT}, task);`
`base::ThreadPool::PostTask(FROM_HERE, {base::MayBlock(), base::TaskPriority::BEST_EFFORT, base::TaskShutdownBehavior::SKIP_ON_SHUTDOWN}, task);`
`base::ThreadPool::PostTask(FROM_HERE, {base::MayBlock(), base::TaskPriority::BEST_EFFORT, base::TaskShutdownBehavior::BLOCK_SHUTDOWN}, task);`
`base::ThreadPool::PostTask(FROM_HERE, {base::MayBlock(), base::TaskPriority::USER_BLOCKING, base::TaskShutdownBehavior::SKIP_ON_SHUTDOWN}, task);`
explain: Explicitly specify `base::TaskPriority` and shutdown behavior instead of relying on defaults — `BEST_EFFORT` for non-urgent work, `SKIP_ON_SHUTDOWN` when it can be abandoned.

prompt: New code needs to encrypt a token before storing it. A teammate writes `OSCrypt::EncryptString(plaintext, &ciphertext);`. What's the review feedback?
choices: Fine, as long as it's called off the UI thread, since it may block on the keychain
Use the async OSCrypt interface (`os_crypt_async`); the sync one is deprecated
Wrap it in `base::ThreadPool::PostTask` so encryption never blocks the UI
Store the token in plain prefs instead; prefs are already protected by the OS
explain: New code must use the async OSCrypt interface; the legacy synchronous `OSCrypt` interface is deprecated.

prompt: A component-level `DefaultBrowserMonitor` needs platform-specific "is default browser?" logic. Which design does the standard prefer?
choices: Store a `base::RepeatingCallback<bool()> is_default_browser_callback_` passed in by the platform layer
Add `#if BUILDFLAG(IS_WIN)` / `IS_MAC` blocks directly in the component class
A nested `Delegate` interface (`virtual bool IsDefaultBrowser() = 0;`) owned via `std::unique_ptr`
Have the component include the browser-layer shell-integration header directly
explain: For cross-layer platform behavior, use a dedicated delegate class rather than raw callbacks — cleaner interfaces, safer lifetimes, and better testability.

prompt:
Reviewing:

```cpp
remote_.set_disconnect_handler(
    base::BindOnce(&MyClass::OnDisconnect,
                   base::Unretained(this)));
void MyClass::OnDisconnect() { remote_.reset(); }
```

What's the best suggestion?
choices: Replace with `remote_.reset_on_disconnect();`
Replace `base::Unretained(this)` with a WeakPtr — it's a UaF
Call `remote_.reset()` in the destructor too
No change; this is the idiomatic pattern
explain: When the disconnect handler only resets the remote, use the built-in `remote.reset_on_disconnect()` instead of a manual handler.

prompt: A feature needs to remember a list of tabs to close later. Which member type is preferred?
choices: `std::vector<content::WebContents*> tabs_to_close_;`
`std::vector<raw_ptr<content::WebContents>> tabs_to_close_;`
`std::vector<std::string> tabs_to_close_;` holding each tab's URL
`std::vector<tabs::TabHandle> tabs_to_close_;`
explain: Store `tabs::TabHandle`s (integer IDs) rather than `WebContents*`; raw pointers can dangle and be reused for a different allocation, but handles can't accidentally point to a different tab.

prompt: A new mojom method lets the renderer-hosted WebUI ask the browser to fetch data: `FetchResource(url.mojom.Url url)`. The browser only ever needs to fetch from three known endpoints. What should the reviewer suggest?
choices: Add a doc comment stating that the URL must be validated by the browser
Restrict the input to an enum/allowlist of the known endpoints
Accept the URL as a `string` instead of `url.mojom.Url` and parse it browser-side
Nothing; the browser process is trusted, so fetching any URL is fine
explain: Mojom interfaces taking URLs from less-privileged processes should consider an allowlist or enum — an unrestricted URL lets the renderer send requests to any endpoint.

prompt: A mojom method accepts a URL from the renderer, and the browser-side implementation already filters it against an allowlist downstream. Nearby similar methods have no URL-validation comments. Should the reviewer request a doc comment about URL validation?
choices: Yes; every URL parameter in a mojom interface must document its validation
Yes, and also require a second validation step in the mojom traits
No; it's validated downstream and nearby code has no such comments
No, but require converting the parameter to a string to avoid parsing bugs
explain: Never request URL-validation doc comments if the implementation already validates downstream; check surrounding code first, or you introduce inconsistency and verbosity.

prompt: `service->ForEach()` takes a `base::FunctionRef<void(Item&)>`. A test just wants to iterate without doing anything. Which compiles and follows the standard?
choices: `service->ForEach(base::DoNothing());`
`service->ForEach([](Item&) {});`
`service->ForEach(base::NullCallback());`
`service->ForEach(nullptr);`
explain: `base::DoNothing()` doesn't match `base::FunctionRef<void(T&)>` signatures; use an explicit no-op lambda instead.

choices: Fine — a non-null ID guarantees the task still exists in the service
Wrap `actor_service_` in a WeakPtr, since the service may be destroyed first
Add `DCHECK(task_id_)` before the call to document the invariant
Null-check `GetTask()`'s result before calling `Pause()`; it may be gone
explain: Always null-check return values from methods that can return nullptr — a valid ID doesn't guarantee the lookup succeeds. When chaining `a->GetB()->DoC()`, store and check the intermediate.

choices: `model_key` is used after move; don't move it (pass by const ref)
Nothing — the move is inside an `if`, so it only matters on one branch
`std::move(*result)` should be `result.value()` to avoid UB on empty optionals
`callback` should be `std::move`d into `Run()` to avoid a copy
explain: Never use a variable after `std::move()` — it's in a valid but unspecified state. This applies even when the move is inside a branch.

prompt: Which signature follows the standard for a function that inspects a `Foo` without changing ownership and that requires a non-null value?
choices: `void Process(const std::unique_ptr<Foo>& foo);`
`void Process(const scoped_refptr<Foo>& foo);`
`void Process(Foo& foo);`
`void Process(std::unique_ptr<Foo> foo);`
explain: Don't pass smart pointers by const reference — it forces heap allocation and couples callers to an ownership model. Use `T*` or `T&` (when non-null is required).

prompt: A teammate makes a class `base::RefCountedThreadSafe` because it's accessed from two threads and they're unsure who should delete it. What's the guidance?
choices: Good choice; thread-safe refcounting removes lifetime concerns across both threads
Use `std::shared_ptr` instead; its atomic refcount is the standard C++ equivalent
Redesign for single ownership; if refcounting is truly needed, keep it on one sequence
Make it a leaky global singleton (`base::NoDestructor`) so it's never deleted mid-use
explain: Refcounting makes ownership and destruction order hard to reason about, especially across threads. Prefer a redesign with single ownership; otherwise pin to one sequence, proxy via `PostTask()`, and use `WeakPtr` binds.

prompt:
A class caches a pref dict for later use:

```cpp
dict_ = &pref_service_->GetDict(kMyPref);  // const base::Value::Dict*
```

What should it do instead?
choices: Store it as a `raw_ptr<const base::Value::Dict>` for UaF detection
Store a `.Clone()` of the dict by value, or read it inline when needed
Store it as a `const base::Value::Dict&` member bound in the constructor
It's fine — the `PrefService` outlives this class, so the pointer stays valid
explain: Never hold pointers to a `base::Value` returned from `PrefService` — it dangles when the pref updates or the service is destroyed. Clone it for longer-lived use, or use it inline.

prompt: `map_` holds `std::string_view` keys pointing into strings stored in `strings_`. Which declaration order is safe?
choices: Either; destruction order of members is unspecified
Either, as long as the destructor calls `map_.clear()` first
explain: Members are destroyed in reverse declaration order, so declare the depended-upon member (`strings_`) first; it is then destroyed last.

prompt: Sequence-aware code needs per-sequence cached state. A teammate adds `thread_local std::string cache;`. What's the guidance?
choices: Fine — `thread_local` is the C++ standard tool, and a sequence maps to one thread
Wrap it in `base::NoDestructor` and keep `thread_local`, which avoids exit-time destructors
Use `thread_local raw_ptr<std::string>`, since a pointer is trivially destructible
Use `base::SequenceLocalStorageSlot`; `thread_local` needs trivially destructible types
explain: Prefer `base::SequenceLocalStorageSlot` for sequence-aware code. `thread_local` requires trivially destructible types (not `raw_ptr`), no `COMPONENT_EXPORT`, and `ABSL_CONST_INIT` at namespace/class scope.

prompt: A class must always hold a valid, never-changing reference to its `BrowserWindowInterface`, passed into the constructor as `BrowserWindowInterface&`. Which field declaration is preferred?
choices: `BrowserWindowInterface& window_;`
`raw_ptr<BrowserWindowInterface> window_;`
`const raw_ref<BrowserWindowInterface> window_;`
`raw_ref<BrowserWindowInterface> window_;`
explain: Use `const raw_ref<T>` for fields that must never be null (the `const` prevents rebinding, like `T&`); `raw_ptr<T>` is the default for nullable/reassignable non-owning fields.

prompt: A constructor stores `browser->GetProfile()` (which effectively never returns null) into a field, and the author wraps it in `CHECK_DEREF(...)`. When is `CHECK_DEREF` appropriate?
choices: Always — every pointer-to-reference conversion into a `raw_ref` needs `CHECK_DEREF`
Only when the pointer could really be null; here it's a redundant check
Never — plain `*ptr` is equivalent, since a null deref crashes anyway
Only inside tests, where a crash message is more useful than a deref
explain: `CHECK_DEREF` asserts non-null and is safer than `*ptr`, but don't use it reflexively: reserve it for pointers that could really be null, not ones like `GetProfile()` that upstream doesn't check.

choices: Fine — `BindOnce` copies bound arguments, so the string data is safe
Fine — the WeakPtr cancels the task if anything is destroyed
Use `base::Unretained(this)` instead, since the WeakPtr is what can dangle
Bind an owning `std::string(name)`; copying a view copies only the pointer
explain: `base::Bind*` doesn't catch view types like `std::string_view`/`base::span`. Bind an owning copy (`std::string`, `std::vector`), unless using `base::raw_span` or the storage is static.

prompt: Which of these bound view arguments is acceptable per the standard?
choices: A naked `base::span<const uint8_t>` over a local `std::vector` in a posted task
A `base::span` over a `constexpr` static array
A `std::string_view` of a `std::string` parameter
A `base::span` over a member vector bound with `base::Unretained`
explain: Binding a view is OK only with `base::raw_span<T>` (dangling protection) or when the backing storage is static, like a `constexpr` array or a string literal.

prompt:
A class holds a `PrefChangeRegistrar` member and registers:

```cpp
pref_change_registrar_.Add(kSomePref,
    base::BindRepeating(&MyClass::OnPrefChanged,
                        base::Unretained(this)));
```

A linter flags every `base::Unretained(this)`. What's correct?
choices: Safe — the registrar is a member destroyed with `this`; don't flag it
Flag it — `PrefChangeRegistrar` callbacks can run after `this` and need a WeakPtr
Flag it only if the registrar observes `local_state`, which outlives profiles
Flag it — bind `base::DoNothing()` instead and read the pref on demand
explain: `base::Unretained(this)` is safe when the callback is owned by `this` or a member destroyed with it (registrars, timers, owned Mojo endpoints, `CallbackListSubscription`). Only flag it when the callback can outlive `this`.

prompt: Which signature correctly expresses that `SetDelegate` takes ownership of the delegate?
choices: `void SetDelegate(Delegate* delegate);` with `delegate_.reset(delegate)` inside
`void SetDelegate(Delegate& delegate);`
`void SetDelegate(std::unique_ptr<Delegate> delegate);`
`void SetDelegate(const std::unique_ptr<Delegate>& delegate);`
explain: Pointer types in signatures are the ownership contract: `std::unique_ptr<T>` means the function takes ownership. A function must never take ownership of a `T*` parameter.

prompt: A function builds a local `std::unique_ptr<Foo> foo` and returns it. A teammate writes `return std::move(foo);`. Also, a separate function returns a plain moveable value type wrapped in `std::unique_ptr`. What's the guidance?
choices: Both are correct; explicit `std::move` makes the transfer of ownership clear
Use `return foo;` (`std::move` blocks elision) and return moveable types by value
Keep `return std::move(foo);`, but return value types as raw `T*` to avoid copies
Use `std::shared_ptr` for both returns so callers can share the result freely
explain: Don't `std::move()` a local on return — it suppresses copy elision. And a smart pointer isn't the default way to move a value: take or return moveable types by value.

choices: Add `::CloseHandle(file)` before every early return to avoid the leak
Wrap it in `std::unique_ptr<HANDLE>` so it's freed automatically
Use `base::win::ScopedHandle` so it's closed on destruction
Use `base::mac::ScopedCFTypeRef` so the same code is portable
explain: Don't manage OS handles by hand; use platform scopers such as `base::win::ScopedHandle` and `base::apple::ScopedCFTypeRef<T>`, which release on destruction.
